objectives: Trace dance notation from Feuillet (1700) to motion capture.
Read Labanotation + Effort-Shape + Benesh systems at first principles.
Decide when notation, video or mocap is the right documentation.

slides.title: Writing the dance — Feuillet, Stepanov + the long road to Laban
slides.body:
Choreography vanishes the moment the dancer stops. Notation is the attempt to make the dance survive its first performance.

**Pre-modern systems**:
- **Thoinot Arbeau** *Orchésographie* (1588). Step-name + tablature alignment with melody. Early but ad-hoc.
- **Raoul-Auger Feuillet** *Chorégraphie* (Paris 1700). Commissioned within the institutional frame of Louis XIV's Académie Royale de Danse (1661 — P89 L1). Feuillet drew floor patterns on the page + attached symbols for steps + arm gestures along the track. Used widely through the 18C; preserves ~350 baroque dances (minuet, gigue, sarabande). The first widely circulated notation.
- **Pierre Beauchamp** claimed prior invention (Beauchamp-Feuillet system).
- 18-19C: many systems proposed, none universal. The information gap means most pre-Petipa choreography is lost.

**Stepanov notation** (Vladimir Stepanov, *Alphabet des mouvements du corps humain*, Paris 1892). A music-stave-style system used at the Mariinsky Imperial Ballet to record the Petipa repertoire including *The Sleeping Beauty* + *Swan Lake* + *Raymonda*. Brought to London by Nikolai Sergeyev in 1918 → the Sergeyev notations now at Harvard. These are the primary documentary source for reconstructing late-19C Petipa choreography today. Without Stepanov, the surviving Petipa we know is mediated through oral transmission + 20C re-stagings.

**Limitations of pre-Laban notation**: most systems recorded steps + floor paths but not torso, dynamics, effort, simultaneity of multiple dancers, music alignment in detail. Recording 'what the legs did' is not recording the dance.

The 20C demand: a notation that captures the whole moving body in space + time + effort, in any movement vocabulary.

slides.title: Laban — Labanotation + Effort-Shape
slides.body:
**Rudolf Laban** (1879-1958), Austro-Hungarian movement theorist + choreographer (Mary Wigman + Kurt Jooss were students). Two intertwined contributions.

**Labanotation (Kinetography Laban)** — publicly introduced 1928 in *Schrifttanz*. A vertical-staff system read from bottom to top (= time flows upward like a player-piano roll). Columns represent body parts (centre = support; outer columns = limbs in standard order). Symbols encode:
- **Direction** — shape of the symbol (forward = bottom-rounded; right = right-angled; etc.).
- **Level** — shading of the symbol (white = low / floor; striped = middle; black = high / jumped).
- **Duration** — vertical length of the symbol on the staff (long symbol = long count).
- **Body part** — column the symbol sits in.

Labanotation can capture any movement vocabulary, not only ballet — it works on Graham, Cunningham, hip-hop, contact improvisation. Notation Bureau of Dance Notation Bureau (NYC 1940, Ann Hutchinson Guest + colleagues) trained generations of notators + holds the largest archive. Notable scores: Tudor's *Pillar of Fire*, Balanchine's *Apollo*, Limón's *The Moor's Pavane*, Tharp's *Push Comes to Shove*. **Ann Hutchinson Guest** (1918-2022) is the central figure; her textbook *Labanotation* (1954, multiple editions) is canonical.

**Effort-Shape (Laban Movement Analysis, LMA)** — Laban's second system + the qualitative complement to Labanotation. Where Labanotation records *what* the body did, Effort-Shape records *how* it did it. Two axes:

- **Effort**: four factors each on a binary — **Weight** (strong / light) × **Time** (sudden / sustained) × **Space** (direct / indirect) × **Flow** (bound / free). The eight named **Effort Actions** (P89 L3) — punch, slash, press, wring, dab, flick, glide, float — are combinations of weight + time + space.
- **Shape**: how the body's form changes — opening / closing, rising / sinking, advancing / retreating; carving the kinesphere.

**LMA + the Bartenieff Fundamentals** (Irmgard Bartenieff, Laban's student) — applied to dance, theatre, somatic therapy, psychology + later to animation + robotics. LMA is one of the most influential analytical languages outside its native discipline.

slides.title: Benesh + Eshkol-Wachman + Sutton + computer-era documentation
slides.body:
**Benesh Movement Notation** (Rudolf + Joan Benesh, London 1955). Designed at the Royal Ballet to record specifically the ballet vocabulary. Horizontal five-line stave like music. The dancer is seen *from behind* by the notator. Symbols for head, arms, hands, legs + feet are placed on the stave; floor plans + travel direction added in margins. Reads left-to-right with the music. Adopted as the Royal Ballet's house notation; Royal Academy of Dance certifies notators; widely used in ballet contexts. Particularly strong for the upper-body carriage + port de bras that Labanotation captures more cumbersomely.

**Eshkol-Wachman Movement Notation** (Noa Eshkol + Avraham Wachman, Israel 1958, *Movement Notation*). Pure geometry: the body's joints in a coordinate system. Each segment given a coordinate change between sphere-positions. Independent of style or vocabulary; the most mathematically rigorous notation. Used by Eshkol's own Chamber Dance Group (their *Suite for the Solo Dancer* (1953)) + by ethologists studying primate behaviour + by physical therapists. Limited adoption in mainstream choreography because of its abstraction but historically + analytically central.

**Sutton Movement Writing + DanceWriting** (Valerie Sutton, San Diego, from 1966). Stick-figure pictographic notation. Same family of systems that gave us SignWriting for deaf sign languages (also Sutton). Approachable + visual; widely used in education + community contexts. Less precise than Laban or Benesh for nuance but the most read-at-sight.

**Other modern systems**: Massine notation, Conté, Morris's Hanya Holm-derived system; many regional + company-internal.

**Computer + digital era**:
- **LabanWriter** (Ohio State; 1980s+) + **LabanXML** (2000s) — computer-assisted Labanotation + interchange.
- **DanceForms** (formerly LifeForms, Credo Interactive, Vancouver 1989+). Cunningham used it to compose phrases inside a 3D body editor; it became part of his late choreographic process. Forsythe's *Improvisation Technologies* CD-ROM (1999 — P89 L2) is a parallel digital pedagogy artifact.
- **Video capture** (ubiquitous since 1980s). Most choreographers now record rehearsals on phone or fixed camera + use video as the primary working archive. Video preserves dynamics + effort that notation skips, but the camera angle freezes one viewpoint + needs the choreographer to interpret it.
- **Multi-camera + edited archival video** (NY Public Library Dance Division, Pina Bausch Foundation, Crystal Pite tour archives). The Library of Congress + the New York Public Library Jerome Robbins Dance Division hold the largest dance video archives.
- **Motion capture (mocap)**. Optical markers (Vicon, OptiTrack) or markerless (Theia, OpenPose); inertial suits (Xsens, Rokoko). Records joint positions at 60-240 Hz. Used by Wayne McGregor + Random International (P89 L8) + by AI choreography research (Google *Living Archive*, Microsoft *Dance Diffuser* — P89 L8). Resolves dynamics + 3D space but loses dramatic context, costume, music alignment.

**Choosing documentation**:
- **Notation** (Laban + Benesh) survives independent of technology + can be read centuries later; preserves structural + qualitative information.
- **Video** captures dynamics, dramaturgy, costume; depends on playback technology + camera viewpoint.
- **Motion capture** gives spatial + temporal precision usable by computers; loses dramatic context.
- **Combined** (video + score + mocap + rehearsal notes) is the contemporary best practice for major works. Pina Bausch Foundation pioneered the post-mortem archive model after Bausch's 2009 death; Cunningham Trust + Forsythe Company use mixed-media archives. The 21C choreographer documents in three or four media simultaneously.

question.question: Choose the right documentation for four distinct works
question.goal: For four works with different requirements, choose the primary documentation medium + justify.

steps.prompt: Work A: Petipa-era classical ballet you want to be reconstructable in 100 years.

acceptedAnswers: Benesh notation (or Stepanov for historical fidelity) plus archival video

steps.reveal: Benesh Movement Notation — designed at the Royal Ballet for the ballet vocabulary; preserves port de bras + carriage cleanly. Combine with archival video for dynamic reference. For very-historical Petipa reconstruction, Stepanov scores (1892+, Sergeyev archives at Harvard) provide period-correct primary sources.

steps.prompt: Work B: a Cunningham-style chance work with multiple variant orderings.

acceptedAnswers: Labanotation plus DanceForms / computer score; the variant rules captured as algorithm

steps.reveal: Labanotation for the individual movement units + DanceForms (or successor 3D-body editor) for the ordering algorithm + the variant rules captured separately as a written score. Cunningham himself used DanceForms (formerly LifeForms) to compose. Video alone would not capture the *space of possible orderings* — only one realisation.

steps.prompt: Work C: a Pina Bausch Tanztheater work in which gesture + scenography + autobiography are inseparable.

acceptedAnswers: multi-camera video archive plus rehearsal notes; Bausch Foundation model

steps.reveal: Multi-camera video archive plus extensive rehearsal notes + interviews with original dancers + scenography documentation. The Pina Bausch Foundation built this model after Bausch's 2009 death. Notation alone would not capture the autobiographical + sociological texture; Tanztheater is more than its steps.

steps.prompt: Work D: a Wayne McGregor work using motion-capture data as part of the choreographic process.

acceptedAnswers: the mocap dataset itself plus video plus the choreographic process notes

steps.reveal: Preserve the original motion-capture stream (the joint-trajectory dataset) — it *is* the choreography in machine-readable form + can be replayed by any future avatar / dancer / model. Combine with video + the process notes that capture the prompt + selection criteria. This is the model used by McGregor with Random International + Google Arts & Culture's *Living Archive* (P89 L8).

question.question: Which two systems did Rudolf Laban contribute to dance documentation + analysis?
options: Labanotation (Kinetography Laban, 1928) + Effort-Shape / Laban Movement Analysis (LMA). Labanotation is the quantitative system: a vertical staff in which symbols encode direction (shape), level (shading), duration (length) + body part (column). LMA is the qualitative system: Effort (weight × time × space × flow → eight Effort Actions punch / slash / press / wring / dab / flick / glide / float) + Shape (how the body's form changes). Together they capture *what* + *how* the body moves in any vocabulary. Ann Hutchinson Guest (1918-2022) is the central transmitter of Labanotation; Irmgard Bartenieff carried LMA forward. Influence extends to dance, theatre, somatic therapy, animation + robotics.
question.explanation: Laban gave us Labanotation (Kinetography Laban, 1928) for quantitative recording + Effort-Shape / Laban Movement Analysis for qualitative analysis. Benesh (1955) is Rudolf + Joan Benesh's separate system at the Royal Ballet. Sutton (1966) + Eshkol-Wachman (1958) + Stepanov (1892) + Feuillet (1700) are all distinct systems.
hints: Two systems, one quantitative + one qualitative.
question.workedSolution: Rudolf Laban (1879-1958) created Labanotation (Kinetography Laban) in 1928 + the qualitative Effort-Shape / Laban Movement Analysis framework. Labanotation uses a vertical staff with symbols for direction (shape), level (shading), duration (length), body part (column). Effort-Shape encodes weight × time × space × flow → eight named Effort Actions (punch / slash / press / wring / dab / flick / glide / float). Carried forward by Ann Hutchinson Guest (Labanotation) + Irmgard Bartenieff (LMA). Influence reaches dance, theatre, somatic therapy, animation, robotics.

question.question: Building an archive for a major touring company
question.prompt: You are appointed the archivist for a 40-year-old contemporary dance company whose founder + artistic director has just died. The company holds 60 works ranging from pure-movement abstracts to Tanztheater-scale productions with live music + scenography. The board wants the works to be revivable + licensable in 50 years. Outline a 3-medium documentation protocol (notation, video, mocap or supplements) for each major category of work, the staffing + skills you need to recruit, the storage + interchange formats you choose (LabanXML? video codecs? FBX or BVH for mocap?), + the one work-type that will resist every documentation strategy + why.

question.question: A motion-capture session records 30 joint markers at 120 Hz for 10 minutes. Each marker stores x, y, z each as a 4-byte float. Compute the raw data volume in megabytes (1 MB = 10⁶ bytes). Round to nearest integer.
question.hint: 30 markers × 3 coords × 4 bytes × 120 samples/s × 600 s ≈ 2.59 × 10⁸ bytes.

question.prompt: In ≤150 words, explain why no single documentation medium captures a dance + how a 21C choreographer should combine notation, video + mocap. Name Feuillet, Laban, Benesh + one digital system.
question.rubric: Should articulate: notation (Feuillet 1700; Stepanov 1892; Laban 1928; Benesh 1955; Eshkol-Wachman 1958; Sutton 1966) preserves structural + spatial + temporal information independent of recording technology + readable centuries later, but typically loses dynamics + dramaturgy + costume. Video preserves dynamics + dramaturgy + costume but is camera-viewpoint-locked + technology-dependent. Mocap (Vicon, Xsens, OpenPose) gives 3D joint trajectories usable by computers + for AI work (Wayne McGregor, *Living Archive*, *Dance Diffuser* — P89 L8) but loses dramatic context. Best practice = combined archive: Labanotation or Benesh score (preserves structure) + multi-camera video (preserves dynamics + context) + mocap (preserves machine-readable spatial data) + rehearsal notes + interviews. Pina Bausch Foundation, Cunningham Trust + the NY Public Library Dance Division pioneered this combined-media model.
